full_judgment:
Quamrul Islam Siddiqui, J: This Rule was issued on an application for revision made by the pre-emptee-petitioner under section 115(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) against the judgment and order dated 28-9-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. 2nd Court, Madaripur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1995 affirming the judgment and order dated 13-4-1995 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Shibehar, in Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1983. 

 2. The pre-emptor filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1983 in order to have the case land by way of pre-emption. 

 3. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that he is a co-sharer tenant by purchase in the case jama. Opposite party No. 3 (in original miscellaneous case) transferred 1.46 acres of land to the pre-emptor by a registered kabala dated 30-5-1999 and, as such, the pre-emptor became co-sharer by purchase in the case jama. Opposite party No. 3 (in original miscellaneous case) again transferred .60 acre of land to opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 (also in original miscellaneous case) by a registered kabala dated 4-9-1979. But no notice of transfer was served upon the pre-emptor and other co-sharers. Opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are stranger purchasers in the case jama. For the reasons stated, the pre-emptor filed the miscellaneous case for pre-emption. 

 4. Opposite party No. 2 contested the pre-emption case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations made in the application for pre-emption. 

 5. The case of pre-emptee-opposite party No. 2, in short, is that opposite party No. 3 transferred the case land to opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 by a registered Kabala dated 4-9-1979 (Kabala executed on 21-5-1979). The pre-emptor became a co-share to the case jama on the basis of purchase of land from opposite party No. 3 by kabala dated 30-5-1979. The further case of pre-emptee-opposite party No. 2 is that he purchased the case land prior to the date of purchase of the pre-emptor and, as such, the pre-emptor is not entitled to pre-empt the case land. 

 6. On the pleadings, various issues were framed, including maintainability of the miscellaneous case, defect of parties, limitation and whether or not the pre-emptor was entitled to any relief as prayed for. 

 8. Considering the evidence on record, the trial Court allowed the miscellaneous case. On an appeal there from at the instance of pre-emptee No. 2, the Court of appeal below also affirmed the judgment and order passed by the learned Assistant Judge. 

 10. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptee-petitioner, submits that the pre-emptor became a co-sharer in the case jama on the basis of purchase of land from opposite party No. 3 by kabala dated 30-5-1979 and that the kabala dated 21-5-1979 of pre-emptee No. 2 was prior to the kabala of the preemptor. He further submits that since the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2 was executed earlier than the kabala of the pre-emptor, the pre-emptor cannot pre-empt the land of pre-emptee No. 2. He lastly submits that according to section 47 of the Registration Act, registered document operates from the date of its execution and not from date of its registration, and that, as such, the pre-emptor being a subsequent purchaser cannot pre-empt the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2. 

 11. Mr Md Mojibur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the kabala of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 was not executed on 21-5-1979, but it was executed earlier. He further submits that the kabala dated 21-5-1979 of pre-emptee-opposite party No. 2 was antedated and that the same was created with a malaise intention to frustrate the statutory right of pre-emption of the pre-emptor. He lastly submits that considering the evidence on record both the Courts below allowed the miscellaneous case and that, as such, this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code should not interfere with the concurrent findings of facts arrived at by the Courts below. 

 13. It appears that the miscellaneous case was earlier remanded by this Court as per the judgment passed in Civil Revision No. 1010 of 1986. In that judgment, this Court directed to ascertain which of the two kabalas, one standing in the name of the pre-emptor and the other in the name of pre-emptee No. 2, was of earlier date. This Court also give further direction to consider the original kabalas of both the pre-emptor and pre-emptee No.2 in order to ascertain which kabala was of earlier date. According to the direction of this Court, both the original kabalas were filed in the trial Court and the kabala of the pre-emptor was proved and marked as Exhibit No. 1(A) and the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2 (kabala under pre-emption) was marked as Exhibit No. B. The trial Court held that the kabala of the pre-emptor., Exhibit No.1(A), executed on 30-5-1979 was presented for registration on 30-5-1979 and that it was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 27-12-1979. The trial Court further held that the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2 (Exhibit No. B), executed on 21-5-1979 was presented for registration on 4-9-1979 and that it was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 16-1-1980. So, the trial Court held that as the kabala of the pre-emptor was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 27-12-1979 and as the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2 was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 16-1-1980, the kabala of the pre-emptor was a prior kabala to the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2. 

 17. It appears that both the Courts below held that right of pre-emption accrues from the date of registration of the kabala under section 60 of the Registration Act, not from the date of its execution. There is no dispute that the right of pre-emption accrues from the date of registration, not from the date of execution of the kabala. In fact, date of registration of a kabala under section 60 of the Registration Act is taken into consideration for the purpose of computation of limitation in filing a miscellaneous case for pre-emption. According to section 47 of the Registration Act, registered document dates back to its date of execution and operates from that date. There is a long line of decisions which have settled that registered document operates from the date of its execution and not from the date of its registration. In support of this contention, reliance may be placed on the case of Rafiqul Islam (Md) vs Mir Abdul Ali, 44 DLR (AD) 176. In the case referred to above, the Appellate Division has held that sale deed executed earlier but registered later in point of time will prevail over sale deed executed later but registered earlier. The criterion in such cases for the purpose of determining when the sale takes effect is not the date of registration but the date of execution of the deed itself. 

 18. The principle expressed in the case referred to above fully applies in the facts and circumstances of the case in hand. After execution of the deed, normally the vendee is inducted into possession of the land sold, but after presentation of a document for registration it takes days, months and even years to get a document registered under section 60 of the Registration Act. There is no hand of the seller or purchaser in the process of completion of registration. It is the domain of the registration authority to complete registration of a deed. The seller is free after execution and presentation of the deed for registration. It is a common practice that after execution and presentation of the deed for registration, the purchaser is inducted into possession of the land sold. In a pre-emption case, we have to see whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer to the case jama or not. Here, in the case in hand, both the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee claim that they are co-sharers by purchase and their common vendor is opposite party No. 3. According to section 47 of the Registration Act, the deed executed earlier must take precedence over the deed executed later. After registration of the deed it takes effect from the date of its execution. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-opposite parties contended that pre-emptee No. 2 took more than 3 months' time to present the deed for registration after its execution and this unusual delay casts serious doubt about the genuineness of the date of execution of the deed of pre-emptee No. 2. In reply, learned Advocate for pre-emptee No. 2 submitted that according to section 23 of the Registration Act, a deed could be presented for registration within 4 months from the date of its execution. 

 21. It appears that from the amended section 23, the limitation for presentation of a deed for registration after execution is 3 months instead of 4 months. Since the kabala under pre-emption was executed on 21-5-1979, unlamented section 23 will be applicable in the present case. Therefore, pre-emptee No. 2 has not committed any wrong in presenting his kabala after more than 3 months of its execution. Because, at the relevant time the limitation for presentation of a document for registration was 4 months after its execution. It appears that pre-emptee No. 2 presented the deed dated 21-5-1979 for registration after its execution within the stipulated period of 4 months. 

 22. It also appears that the kabala of pre-emptee No. 2 was executed earlier than the kabala of the pre-emptor. Therefore, according to section 47 of the Registration Act, the deed of pre-emptee No. 2 was earlier than the kabala of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor became a co-sharer to the case jama on 30-5-1979, pre-emptee No. 2 became a co-sharer on 21-5-1979. The preemptor was not even a co-sharer in the case holding when the pre-emptee became a co-sharer on 21-5-1979. In order to exercise the right of pre-emption, one must be a co-sharer firs, then the question of accrual of right of pre-emption arises. Since pre-emptee No. 2 became a co-sharer in the case holding earlier than the pre-emptor, no miscellaneous case for pre-emption lies against him. Therefore, the pre-emptor cannot legally pre-empt the land purchased by pre-emptee No. 2. This important legal aspect was not considered by both the Courts below. Therefore, the judgments of the Courts below cannot sustain in law. 

 25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Court of appeal below affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court is set aside and the miscellaneous case is dismissed.
